name: David Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpentry foreman for a commercial fit-out contractor, so we take empty office floors and shop units in the city centre and turn them into offices, cafés and stores. This month it's a restaurant: bespoke timber booths, a curved bar front and wall panelling, with a crew of six carpenters plus whoever the other trades send. Shop fits run on tight deadlines, so some weeks I'm on nights, starting at eight in the evening when the mall's closed. I love the pressure and the look on the owner's face at handover; what wears me out is the night shifts and drawings that arrive half-finished.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you organise all that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On my phone, mostly with AI. I use an assistant every day to break drawings down into cut lists, plan the crew's week, write the daily reports and check fire regulations for the panels. I'm a bit of a gadget guy; I've got a laser measure that talks to my phone. Outside work, I go to church with my girlfriend Ingrid most Sundays, and we're talking about getting engaged next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. We call it AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's a great tool, and the people who called it the end of the world were wrong. I'd say it at work and probably on the trade forums I post on. Tools come and go; good tradesmen stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my head start matters a bit and that's all. I'm faster on the admin than most foremen, which is why the boss gives me the tricky jobs. I'd keep climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep using the tools, and in a year or two I'd set up my own small fit-out firm. I've got about five months saved and a couple of clients who'd come with me. I'd want to buy a decent van and a track saw kit, maybe ten thousand all in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, ready to get on with it. It's the kind of future I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your own firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather build something than work for someone else forever. My granddad ran a joinery shop for forty years and he always said, be your own man if you can. The market rewards people who take the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clients not paying, mainly, fit-out is famous for it. You do the work, they hold the last ten percent for months. I'd keep a cushion and be careful who I work for.

S0.say: I'd say AI's a great tool and the doom-mongers were wrong, at work and on the trade forums I post on. Tools come and go; good tradesmen stay.
S0.think: Privately my head start matters a bit and that's all: I'm faster on admin than most foremen, which is why I get the tricky jobs. I'd keep climbing.
S0.do: Keeps working and using AI tools daily, then in a year or two sets up his own small fit-out firm with clients who'd follow him. Spends about 10,000 of his five months of savings on a van and a track saw kit.
S0.feel: Calm and ready to get on with it.
S0.quote: My granddad ran a joinery shop for forty years and he always said, be your own man if you can.
S0.fieldNote: Ambitious and market-minded, with a family example of self-employment behind him. AI is simply part of his toolkit. His concern is late payment, a classic fit-out risk, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how progress works: some jobs go, better ones come, and the people who learn fastest win. I'd say government should keep out of the way and let businesses and colleges train people. I'd post about it on the forums, and I'd probably get into arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's great for me. A small firm with AI planning and robot cutting can undercut the big contractors on speed. I'd be ahead of most people my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the firm within the year, and invest in a CNC router, about twenty thousand on finance, so we can pre-make booths and panels in a small unit. I'd use AI for all the quoting and scheduling, so I wouldn't need an office person. I'd hire two lads and train them on the machines from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly excited. I'd be sketching the unit layout on napkins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twenty thousand on finance with five months saved. Isn't that a gamble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but a calculated one. I've run the numbers: two restaurant fits a quarter and it pays for itself in eighteen months. If I wait until everyone else has one, the advantage is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would lose out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firms that won't change, and older guys who won't learn the machines. I feel for them, but I can't build my life around protecting their way of working. I'd take on any of them who wanted to learn, though.

S1.say: I'd say this is how progress works: some jobs go, better ones come, and fast learners win. Government should keep out of the way and let businesses and colleges train people, and I'd argue about it on the forums.
S1.think: Off the record it's great for me: a small firm with AI planning and robot cutting can undercut the big contractors on speed. I'd be ahead of most people my age.
S1.do: Sets up his own firm within the year and buys a CNC router for about 20,000 on finance to pre-make booths and panels in a small unit. Runs quoting and scheduling with AI instead of hiring office staff and trains two new hires on the machines from day one.
S1.quote: If I wait until everyone else has one, the advantage is gone.
S1.fieldNote: Steady disruption is his opportunity, and his free-market outlook frames the losers as people who won't change. He'd borrow heavily but has run the numbers. He offers a place to older workers willing to learn, a softer note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a massive shake-up and people will have to be resourceful. I'd still say the market will create new things, though I'd be less sure than I sound. Churches and families will have to carry a lot of people, and maybe the government a bit, for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. In two years I couldn't build a firm and get the money out before robots do fit-outs cheaper than me. My adaptability gets me a head start, but in a sprint that short, a head start isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't start the firm, too risky. I'd stay employed, push to be the guy who runs any robot kit we get, and save hard. I'd put some savings into shares of the companies making the robots and AI, because if they're taking the work, I want a slice of what they earn. Ingrid and I would probably push the engagement back a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Fired up and nervous at the same time, like the night before a big handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said less sure than you sound. Say more about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I believe in markets, I do. But a market where machines do everything isn't one I understand, and I don't think anyone does. I'd say the confident thing in public and lie awake a bit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ingrid that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're young, we've got savings, we'll be all right, and God hasn't let us down yet. She'd ask if we should still get engaged and I'd say yes, but quietly I'd want to wait and see the money first.

S2.say: I'd say it's a massive shake-up and people will need to be resourceful, and that markets will create new things, though I'd be less sure than I sound. Churches and families would carry many people, and government a bit, for a while.
S2.think: Privately I'd be worried: in two years I couldn't build a firm and profit before robots do fit-outs cheaper. My head start isn't much in a sprint that short.
S2.do: Drops the plan to start a firm, stays employed and pushes to run any robot kit on site while saving hard. Buys shares in companies making robots and AI to get a slice of their earnings, and leans towards delaying the engagement with Ingrid.
S2.feel: Anxious, fired up and nervous at once, like the night before a big handover.
S2.quote: I'd say the confident thing in public and lie awake a bit at home.
S2.fieldNote: A clear gap between his public market confidence and private doubt. His instinct is to own a slice of the companies doing the replacing. Faith and his relationship with Ingrid are where his worry shows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, so use it. Learn the tools, build something, save money. I'd tell the young lads on site not to wait for anyone to rescue them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to build a small firm, run it hard with machines and make decent money before it all changes. Not forever, but enough to buy a house outright or near enough. That's my aim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go out on my own in the first year, borrow for the CNC and a robotic arm for sanding and finishing, and keep the crew small. I'd put a slice of every month's profit into shares in robotics and AI companies. By about 2030 I'd want the firm either sold or turned into a business that hires out robot crews rather than carpenters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I'd be energised. I work best with a deadline over my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hiring out robot crews. Would you feel bad about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I'd be doing to other carpenters what's being done to me. But if I don't, someone else will, and I'd rather it was a local firm that treats people decently than a giant one that doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years compare to two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'm a passenger holding on. With five, I'm driving, even if I can see the end of the road. That's a massive difference for someone like me.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a window, so use it: learn the tools, build something, save money. I'd tell the young lads not to wait for anyone to rescue them.
S3.think: Off the record, five years is enough to build a small firm, run it hard with machines and make enough to buy a house outright or close to it. That's my aim.
S3.do: Goes out on his own in the first year, borrowing for a CNC and a robotic sanding arm, and puts part of each month's profit into robotics and AI shares. Aims by about 2030 to sell the firm or turn it into a business hiring out robot crews.
S3.quote: I'd be doing to other carpenters what's being done to me.
S3.fieldNote: He admits a moral twinge about becoming the one who replaces carpenters, then justifies it as better a decent local firm than a giant. Five years restores his sense of control. Invests both in the business and in the companies driving the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and people who work hard and plan will come through it. Government should be a safety net for those who really can't, but not a hammock. Families and churches will be more important than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about this one. Ten years is enough to build a firm, own the machines, buy a house and put money into the companies that win. By 2036 I'd hope to be an owner, not an employee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the firm in the first year, grow it to maybe ten people by 2030 and add machines each year as they get cheaper. I'd marry Ingrid, buy a house with a sensible mortgage, and invest monthly in shares, especially robotics. I'd also go to evening classes in business management, because running a company is a different skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: It's the same end point as the fast one. Why so calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the danger is in the speed, not the destination. With a decade, I can be on the owning side when it lands. I don't think the world ends when robots do the work; it changes who gets paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your crew in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part. I'd want to give them a share in the firm along the way, so they're owners too when the machines take over. My granddad gave his best man a share of the joinery shop, and I'd like to do that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning, and people who work hard and plan will come through. Government should be a safety net for those who really can't, not a hammock, and families and churches will matter more than ever.
S4.think: Privately I'd feel good: ten years is enough to build a firm, own the machines, buy a house and invest in the winners. By 2036 I'd hope to be an owner, not an employee.
S4.do: Sets up his firm in the first year, grows it to about ten people by 2030 and adds machines yearly. Marries Ingrid, buys a house on a sensible mortgage, invests monthly in robotics shares and takes evening classes in business management.
S4.quote: I don't think the world ends when robots do the work; it changes who gets paid.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he is confident of ending up on the owning side. He frames the real question as who gets paid and answers it with ownership and shares, in line with his market outlook. His plan to give his crew a stake echoes his grandfather.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to get on the owning side. What would help is making it easy for small firms to borrow and buy machines, and helping ordinary workers own shares. And churches and families getting ready to look after people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of my sense of who I am comes from work, but not all of it, and that's what I'd hold on to. A man's worth isn't only his job, even if I forget that some weeks.

headlineQuote: A man's worth isn't only his job, even if I forget that some weeks.
portrait: David is a 27-year-old carpentry foreman for a city-centre commercial fit-out contractor, a gadget lover who uses AI every day and goes to church with his girlfriend Ingrid. Inspired by his grandfather's joinery shop, he wants to run his own firm and believes the market rewards those who take risks. He is calm and excited in the mild pictures, ready to borrow for machines. Fast AGI makes him anxious and he admits his public confidence hides private doubt, so he stays employed and buys shares in robot makers. With five or ten years he plans to own the machines, invest and give his crew a stake, seeing the real question as who gets paid.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to get on the owning side of the change.
whatWouldHelp: Making it easy for small firms to borrow and buy machines, helping ordinary workers own shares, and churches and families preparing to look after people.
